q: What is the history of radio navigation?
How did radio navigation develop during World War II?
What was LORAN navigation?
What was the Decca navigation system?
What was Omega navigation?
How did GPS replace older radio navigation systems?
What are augmentation systems in satellite navigation?
history of radio navigation LORAN Decca Omega GPS
WAAS EGNOS augmentation systems satellite navigation
a: Radio navigation began with radio direction finding in the early 1900s and accelerated dramatically during World War II with systems like LORAN (Long Range Navigation), which used time differences between pulsed signals from fixed stations to determine position, and Decca, which used phase comparison of continuous wave signals for higher accuracy in coastal waters. These were followed by Omega (a very low frequency worldwide system), VOR and DME for aviation, and ILS for precision approaches, before the Global Positioning System (GPS) revolutionized navigation with global, all-weather, highly accurate positioning using satellite signals. Modern navigation relies on multiple satellite constellations including GPS (US), GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (European Union), and BeiDou (China), with augmentation systems such as WAAS (US), EGNOS (Europe), MSAS (Japan), and GAGAN (India) improving accuracy for aviation through satellite-based correction signals, while resilient navigation concerns have driven renewed interest in eLORAN as a backup for GPS timing and positioning for critical infrastructure.

q: What is VOR navigation?
How does VOR work?
What are the different types of VOR stations?
What is a VOR approach?
What are Victor airways?
What is the VOR Minimum Operational Network?
Is VOR being phased out?

VOR navigation explained
VOR types approaches Victor airways MON phase-out
a: VOR (VHF Omnidirectional Range) operates between 108-117.95 MHz and provides bearing information to aircraft by transmitting two signals whose phase difference indicates the radial (direction from the station), allowing pilots to navigate along specific radials to or from VOR stations. VOR stations are categorized as high altitude (covering up to 45,000 feet over 130 nautical miles), low altitude (covering up to 18,000 feet), and terminal (covering lower altitudes within 25 nautical miles), and they form the backbone of Victor airways—the low-altitude airway system in the United States. VOR is being phased out in favor of GPS-based RNAV navigation, with the US FAA maintaining a Minimum Operational Network (MON) of VORs for backup, but VOR has limitations including line-of-sight signal propagation, terrain masking, signal interference from buildings and power lines, scalloping (signal bending over rough terrain), and site errors from reflections, all of which can cause course deviation indicator (CDI) fluctuations and unreliable guidance.

q: What is DME in aviation?
How does DME work?
What is slant range in DME?
What is a DME arc?
What are DME approaches and fixes?
What is TACAN navigation?
What is VORTAC?
How does DME differ from GPS distance?
DME distance measuring equipment explained
DME arc approaches TACAN VORTAC
a: DME (Distance Measuring Equipment) operates in the UHF band (962-1213 MHz) and measures the slant-range distance between an aircraft and a ground station by calculating the time delay between an interrogation pulse from the aircraft and a reply from the ground station, with DME frequencies paired to VOR frequencies so a single tuning selects both. DME arcs are procedures where aircraft fly a constant distance from a DME station to transition between segments of an instrument approach, requiring the pilot to make successive small heading corrections to maintain the arc, while DME fixes are position definitions based on a radial from a VOR and a distance from a DME station. TACAN (Tactical Air Navigation) is a military system that provides both bearing and distance in a single UHF signal, and VORTAC stations combine a civil VOR with a military TACAN, allowing civilian aircraft to use the VOR for bearing and the TACAN's DME component for distance—though the distance accuracy of DME differs from GPS because DME measures slant range (including altitude) while GPS typically displays horizontal distance.

ILS instrument landing system explained
ILS categories minimums localizer glideslope decision height
a: The Instrument Landing System (ILS) provides precision vertical and horizontal guidance to aircraft approaching a runway, consisting of the localizer (providing lateral guidance on 108-111.975 MHz), the glideslope (providing vertical guidance on paired UHF frequencies), marker beacons (providing distance-to-runway information), and approach lighting systems. ILS approaches are categorized by minimum visibility and decision height requirements: Category I (decision height 200 feet, visibility 2,400 feet or RVR 1,800), Category II (decision height 100 feet, RVR 1,200), and Category III (IIIa: decision height below 100 feet or none, RVR 700; IIIb: RVR 150; IIIc: no RVR limit, no decision height, allowing autoland in zero visibility). ILS limitations include sensitivity to terrain and buildings causing localizer and glideslope beam bends, the expense and maintenance requirements of ground equipment, the limitation of one approach per runway end (frequency congestion), and the fact that only Category I approaches are widely available, with higher categories requiring specialized aircraft equipment and crew certification—leading to the development of GBAS (Ground-Based Augmentation System) and LAAS (Local Area Augmentation System) as satellite-based alternatives that can provide precision approach guidance to multiple runways at once.
